claims.source: We next backcrossed these mice onto Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- double knockout mice to generate hemizygous Irf7-expressing animals (SiglechIrf7/+;Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- referred to as 'pDC:Irf7+' mice).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the mouse model generation.

claims.claim: Use of hemizygous mice preserved one copy of the Siglech gene.
claims.source: Use of hemizygous mice preserved one copy of the Siglech gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the mouse model and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Irf3/7 double knockout mice are deficient in IFN-I production.
claims.source: Irf3/7 double knockout mice (referred to as Irf3/7 DKO mice), deficient in IFN-I production (Rudd et al., 2012; Schilte et al., 2012) were used as comparator negative controls in all experiments.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rudd et al., 2012 and Schilte et al., 2012.

claims.claim: pDCs were the only cell type to retain significant levels of IRF7 protein expression in pDC:Irf7+ mice.
claims.source: pDCs were the only cell type to retain significant levels of IRF7 protein expression, seen in both pDC:Irf7+ and WT mice, but not in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: IFN-I activity was observed in plasma/spleen of WT mice stimulated by TLR9 or TLR3 agonists, whereas little-to-no IFN-I activity was detected in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: As expected, we observed IFN-I activity in plasma/spleen of WT mice stimulated by either agonist, whereas little-to-no IFN-I activity was detected in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claims.claim: pDC:Irf7+ mice produced high levels of IFN-I in response to TLR9, but not TLR3 agonists.
claims.source: Consistent with the TLR expression patterns in pDCs (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015), pDC:Irf7+ mice produced high levels of IFN-I in response to TLR9, but not TLR3 agonists.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data and citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claims.claim: pDC:Irf7+ and WT pDCs produced similar amounts of IFNα when treated with TLR7 agonists or DENV-infected cells.
claims.source: pDC:Irf7+ and WT pDCs produced similar amounts of IFNα (Figures 2E and 3A), confirming the functionality of IRF7 signaling in pDC:Irf7+ mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 2E and 3A.

claims.claim: TNFα secretion levels in response to TLR7 agonists were comparable in pDCs from Irf3/7 DKO, pDC:Irf7+, and WT mice.
claims.source: Confirming independent activation of NF-κB, we observed TNFα secretion levels in both strains to be comparable to WT mice (Figures 2F and 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 2F and 3B.

claims.claim: ISGs previously defined as IRF5-dependent (e.g. Mx1, Ifit1) were still upregulated in Irf3/7 DKO pDCs when cocultured with DENV-infected cells or stimulated by other TLR7 agonists.
claims.source: Of note, ISGs previously defined as IRF5-dependent (e.g. Mx1, Ifit1) (Lazear et al., 2013) were still upregulated in Irf3/7 DKO pDCs when cocultured with DENV-infected cells or stimulated by other TLR7 agonists (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and citation to Lazear et al., 2013.

claims.claim: High levels of IFNα were detected in both the spleen and plasma of DENV-infected WT mice.
claims.source: High levels of IFNα were detected in both the spleen and plasma of infected WT mice (Figure 3C–D), but not Irf3/7 DKO mice, in agreement with previous results (Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C–D and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: IFNα was not detected in the spleen and plasma of DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: High levels of IFNα were detected in both the spleen and plasma of infected WT mice (Figure 3C–D), but not Irf3/7 DKO mice, in agreement with previous results (Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C–D and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: pDC:Irf7+ mice had undetectable IFNα/β levels in both the plasma and spleen at all analyzed times post-infection with DENV.
claims.source: pDC:Irf7+ mice had undetectable IFNα/β levels in both the plasma and spleen at all analyzed times post-infection (p.i.) (Figure 3C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C–D.

claims.claim: Despite undetectable IFNα/β in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, an early induction (i.e. 18 h p.i.) of ISG RNAs was observed in all tissues analyzed.
claims.source: Importantly, despite undetectable IFNα/β in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, an early induction (i.e. 18 h p.i.) of ISG RNAs was observed in all tissues analyzed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Early induction of ISG RNAs was not observed in Irf3/7 DKO mice at 18 h p.i. with DENV.
claims.source: By contrast, this early induction was not observed in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Basal ISG expression levels were lower in Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to WT, likely reflecting diminished basal IFNAR signaling in the absence of Irf3 and Irf7.
claims.source: Of note, basal ISG expression levels were lower in Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to WT, likely reflecting diminished basal IFNAR signaling in the absence of Irf3 and Irf7 (Gough et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and citation to Gough et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Restricted expression of Irf7 in pDCs is sufficient to generate a systemic ISG response.
claims.source: These results indicate that restricted expression of Irf7 in pDCs is sufficient to generate a systemic ISG response.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: DENV infection induced ISGs and NF-κB-dependent transcripts in WT, but not Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: DENV infection induced ISGs and NF-κB-dependent transcripts in WT, but not Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 3E–G; expressed as magnitude-independent Z score and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; expressed as magnitude-dependent fold-change), confirming previous findings (Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 3E–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Despite a strong upregulation of ISGs in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, minimal induction of NF-κB-dependent inflammation-related transcripts was observed.
claims.source: Strikingly, despite a strong upregulation of ISGs in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, we observed minimal induction of NF-κB-dependent inflammation-related transcripts (Figure 3F–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 3F–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The principal signaling pathway downstream of DENV-activated pDCs is IRF7-dependent induction of the IFN-I pathway, which could be wholly segregated from the activation of NF-κB-induced cytokines.
claims.source: Based on these in vivo and ex vivo observations, we concluded that the principal signaling pathway downstream of DENV-activated pDCs is IRF7-dependent induction of the IFN-I pathway, which could be wholly segregated from the activation of NF-κB-induced cytokines.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: At 42–72 hr post-infection, pDC:Irf7+ mice displayed significantly reduced levels of DENV titer and RNA in the spleen and plasma compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: Notably, at 42–72 hr post-infection, pDC:Irf7+ mice displayed significantly reduced levels of DENV titer and RNA in the spleen and plasma compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Viral titer and RNA levels were lower in WT mice than either Irf3/7 DKO or pDC:Irf7+ mice, likely due to the higher IFN-I response.
claims.source: Viral titer and RNA levels were lower in WT mice than either Irf3/7 DKO or pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), likely due to the higher IFN-I response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The higher DENV levels in pDC:Irf7+ mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice at early time points (i.e. 28 h p.i.) may reflect an enhanced recruitment of DENV-susceptible cells in the spleen of pDC:Irf7+ mice due to the localized pDC-induced IFN-I response.
claims.source: The higher DENV levels in pDC:Irf7+ mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice at early time points (i.e. 28 h p.i.) may reflect an enhanced recruitment of DENV-susceptible cells in the spleen of pDC:Irf7+ mice due to the localized pDC-induced IFN-I response (Schmid and Harris, 2014; Seo et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Schmid and Harris, 2014 and Seo et al., 2011.

claims.claim: IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control DENV through the local production of IFN-I.
claims.source: Our results indicate that IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control DENV through the local production of IFN-I.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Ifng and Gbp2 up-regulation temporally correlated with the induction of IFN-I-induced ISGs in DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, Ifng and Gbp2 up-regulation (Figure 5B–C) temporally correlated with the induction of IFN-I-induced ISGs in DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 5A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E.

claims.claim: ISGs including Ifit1/Usp18/Ifit3 respond more highly to IFN-I, but will still be induced to some extent by type II IFN.
claims.source: Of note, these ISGs including Ifit1/Usp18/Ifit3 respond more highly to IFN-I, but will still be induced to some extent by type II IFN [(Chen et al., 2013; Hall et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) and data not shown].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013, Hall et al., 2012, and Liu et al., 2012.

claims.claim: IFN-II signaling likely mediates the late induction of a larger set of ISGs observed in Irf3-/-/7-/- mice.
claims.source: Therefore, in agreement with these prior studies, IFN-II signaling likely mediates the late induction of a larger set of ISGs observed in Irf3-/-/7-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and prior studies.

claims.claim: The kinetic profile of the type II IFN response was markedly different in pDC:Irf7+ mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, with Ifng and Gbp2 expression detected as early as 18 h p.i and peaking at 28 h p.i.
claims.source: The kinetic profile of the type II IFN response was markedly different in pDC:Irf7 +mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, with Ifng and Gbp2 expression detected as early as 18 h p.i and peaking at 28 h p.i. (Figure 5B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figures 5B–C.

claims.claim: Early pDC IRF7-mediated signaling accelerates the IFN-II response, which is known to be part of the eventual control of DENV in mouse models.
claims.source: This led to the compelling hypothesis that early pDC IRF7-mediated signaling accelerates the IFN-II response, which is known to be part of the eventual control of DENV in mouse models (Chen et al., 2013; Costa et al., 2017; Shresta et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013, Costa et al., 2017, and Shresta et al., 2004.

claims.claim: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice abrogated the early ISG response to DENV.
claims.source: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice abrogated this early ISG response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and correspondingly increased both DENV viremia in these mice, as readily observed in the spleen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and to a lesser extent in the blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; not significant; likely as the consequence of the limited dynamic range of DENV detection at this time point in blood).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, C, and D.

claims.claim: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice increased DENV viremia in the spleen.
claims.source: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice abrogated this early ISG response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and correspondingly increased both DENV viremia in these mice, as readily observed in the spleen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and to a lesser extent in the blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; not significant; likely as the consequence of the limited dynamic range of DENV detection at this time point in blood).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: ISG expression was still detected in the Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ at a later time point (72 h p.i.), suggesting that the late induction of ISGs is independent of pDC IRF7-mediated IFN-I and likely induced by IFN-II.
claims.source: Of note, consistent with the results of Figure 5, ISG expression was still detected in the Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ at a later time point (72 h p.i.) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B), further suggesting that the late induction of ISGs is independent of pDC IRF7-mediated IFN-I and likely induced by IFN-II.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: Recent work demonstrates that IRF1-mediated IFN-II can be induced by DENV, independent of Irf3/Irf7 expression.
claims.source: Along the same line, recent work demonstrates that IRF1-mediated IFN-II can be induced by DENV, independent of Irf3/Irf7 expression (Carlin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carlin et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The IFNAR1-dependent response contributes to the control of DENV in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: In accordance, we showed that the IFNAR1-dependent response contributes to the control of DENV in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Despite undetectable IFN-I at a systemic level, the early ISG induction and control of DENV by the pDC-IRF7-induced response relies on IFN-I/IFNAR1 signaling.
claims.source: Together, our results demonstrated that, despite undetectable IFN-I at a systemic level, the early ISG induction and control of DENV by the pDC-IRF7-induced response relies on IFN-I/IFNAR1 signaling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: An acceleration of IFN-II signaling was observed as a result of IRF7 expression in pDCs, temporally associated with viral control in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice.
claims.source: Importantly, we also observed an acceleration of IFN-II signaling as a result of IRF7 expression in pDCs, temporally associated with viral control in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: An elevated fraction (~12%) of splenic NK cells produced IFNγ in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice.
claims.source: We observed that an elevated fraction (~12%) of splenic NK cells produced IFNγ in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: For other cell types, including NKT cells, γδ-T cells, αβ-T cells and neutrophils, IFNγ+ cells represented an extremely small fraction of total splenocytes.
claims.source: For other cell types, including NKT cells, γδ-T cells, αβ-T cells and neutrophils, IFNγ+ cells represented an extremely small fraction of total splenocytes (Figure 6A, right panel and S5A-B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Splenic, but not blood-circulating NK cells, produced IFNγ protein in response to DENV infection.
claims.source: Interestingly, splenic, but not blood-circulating NK cells, produced IFNγ protein in response to DENV infection, consistent with the absence of upregulation of blood Ifng mRNA (data not shown) and limited induction of the activation marker CD69 on blood NK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: NK cell response is localized to the spleen, the primary site of DENV replication.
claims.source: This implies that NK cell response is localized to the spleen, the primary site of DENV replication.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with an early recruitment of neutrophils to the spleen.
claims.source: In agreement with a localized host response, we showed that the accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with an early recruitment of neutrophils to the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) as well as maturation of monocytes (identified as Ly6C++/Lineage- cells), as represented by upregulation of MHCII, which did not occur in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with maturation of monocytes, as represented by upregulation of MHCII, which did not occur in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: In agreement with a localized host response, we showed that the accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with an early recruitment of neutrophils to the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) as well as maturation of monocytes (identified as Ly6C++/Lineage- cells), as represented by upregulation of MHCII, which did not occur in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Both neutrophils and monocytes have been previously shown to be involved in the modulation of NK cell activation.
claims.source: Of note, both cell types have been previously shown to be involved in the modulation of NK cell activation (Costa et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2017 and Kang et al., 2008.

claims.claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice lead to a significant increase of both splenic DENV RNA and viral titers.
claims.source: An efficient depletion of NK cells (i.e. reduction by >80% of splenic and blood NK cells, Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) lead to a significant increase of both splenic DENV RNA and viral titers in pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with a decrease in IFNγ mRNA, IFNγ protein and IFN-II ISG signature in the spleen and plasma.
claims.source: This was associated with a decrease in IFNγ mRNA, IFNγ protein and IFN-II ISG signature in the spleen and plasma (Figure 6D–E), along with reduced neutrophil recruitment to the spleen and maturation of monocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 6D–E.

claims.claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice resulted in reduced neutrophil recruitment to the spleen and maturation of monocytes.
claims.source: This was associated with a decrease in IFNγ mRNA, IFNγ protein and IFN-II ISG signature in the spleen and plasma (Figure 6D–E), along with reduced neutrophil recruitment to the spleen and maturation of monocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C.

claims.claim: IFN-I-induced ISG levels were not impacted by NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice at 48 h p.i.
claims.source: Closing the circle and establishing IFNα responses as upstream, we observed that IFN-I-induced ISG levels were not impacted by NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice at 48 h p.i. (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Human pDCs produced robust IFNα in response to CHIKV only when in contact with CHIKV-infected cells.
claims.source: We tested whether pDC activation by CHIKV shares the same features as DENV, showing that indeed, human pDCs produced robust IFNα in response to CHIKV only when in contact with CHIKV-infected cells (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Robust IFNα levels were detected when WT mouse pDCs were co-cultured with CHIKV infected Vero cells or with syngeneic co-cultures of Irf3/7 DKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs).
claims.source: Similarly, robust IFNα levels were detected when WT mouse pDCs were co-cultured with CHIKV infected Vero cells or with syngeneic co-cultures of Irf3/7 DKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 7B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SiMoA assay data shown in Figures 7B–C.

claims.claim: Cell-free CHIKV and CHIKV-infected cells physically separated from pDCs did not induce IFNα secretion.
claims.source: By contrast, cell-free CHIKV and CHIKV-infected cells physically separated from pDCs did not induce IFNα secretion (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and SiMoA assay data shown in Figures 7A–B.

claims.claim: CHIKV-infected cells failed to activate pDCs deficient for Tlr7.
claims.source: CHIKV-infected cells failed to activate pDCs deficient for Tlr7, whereas pDCs deficient for Mavs (i.e. the downstream signaling adaptor of RLR pathway) produced levels of IFNα comparable to WT pDCs (Figure 7D and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SiMoA assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: pDCs deficient for Mavs produced levels of IFNα comparable to WT pDCs in response to CHIKV-infected cells.
claims.source: CHIKV-infected cells failed to activate pDCs deficient for Tlr7, whereas pDCs deficient for Mavs (i.e. the downstream signaling adaptor of RLR pathway) produced levels of IFNα comparable to WT pDCs (Figure 7D and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SiMoA assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The sensing of CHIKV-infected cells by pDCs led to an IRF7-mediated cytokine production (IFNα), but not NF-κB-induced inflammatory cytokines (TNFα).
claims.source: Comparable to DENV-induced responses, the sensing of CHIKV-infected cells by pDCs led to an IRF7-mediated cytokine production (IFNα), but not NF-κB-induced inflammatory cytokines (TNFα) (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: pDC induction by CHIKV required the cell-to-cell sensing of infected cells by TLR7-induced signaling and led to an IRF7-restricted response.
claims.source: Together, this demonstrated that, like DENV, pDC induction by CHIKV required the cell-to-cell sensing of infected cells by TLR7-induced signaling and led to an IRF7-restricted response.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: WT mice showed no clinical symptoms to CHIKV infection, whereas Irf3/7 DKO mice rapidly succumbed to CHIKV infection.
claims.source: Mice were infected s.c. with CHIKV, and as previously reported WT mice showed no clinical symptoms, whereas Irf3/7 DKO mice rapidly succumbed to CHIKV infection (Figure 7F) (Schilte et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7F and citation to Schilte et al., 2012.

claims.claim: pDC:Irf7+ mice experienced no overt clinical symptoms with 100% of mice surviving CHIKV infection.
claims.source: By contrast, pDC:Irf7+ mice experienced no overt clinical symptoms with 100% of mice surviving infection (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Early control of CHIKV viremia was improved in pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, although reduced as compared to WT mice.
claims.source: Early control of viremia was improved in pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, although reduced as compared to WT mice (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: By day 7 p.i., pDC:Irf7+ mice had cleared CHIKV infections.
claims.source: By day 7 p.i., pDC:Irf7+ mice had cleared CHIKV infections (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown.

claims.claim: There was differential control of CHIKV in pDC:Irf7+ mice depending on the tissue.
claims.source: Importantly, there was differential control of CHIKV in pDC:Irf7+ mice depending on the tissue.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: The initial sites of CHIKV replication (i.e. the infection site: skin/muscle and muscle) displayed relatively higher viral titers as compared to more distal sites (i.e. the spleen and liver), where virus was barely detectable at 48 h p.i. in pDC:Irf7+ mice.
claims.source: The initial sites of CHIKV replication (i.e. the infection site: skin/muscle and muscle) displayed relatively higher viral titers as compared to more distal sites (i.e. the spleen and liver), where virus was barely detectable at 48 h p.i. in pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: The pDC antiviral response may control infection once virus spreads systematically, as previously proposed in the context of Herpes Simplex virus infection.
claims.source: It is possible that the pDC antiviral response controls infection once virus spreads systematically, as previously proposed in the context of Herpes Simplex virus infection (Swiecki et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Swiecki et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Plasma IFNα remained undetectable in CHIKV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice at both 24 and 48 h p.i. using a highly sensitive Single Molecule Assay (SiMoA).
claims.source: We established a mouse IFNα Single Molecule Assay (SiMoA) (Rissin et al., 2010), with a quantification limit at 0.1 pg/ml (i.e. >100 fold increased sensitivity compared to current assays, data not shown). Nonetheless plasma IFNα remained undetectable in CHIKV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice at both 24 and 48 h p.i. (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown, and is supported by citation to Rissin et al., 2010.

claims.claim: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice induced lethality and greatly increased CHIKV viremia.
claims.source: Therefore, we validated the dependence on IFN-I-induced signaling for the control of CHIK by pDCs using IFNAR1 blocking antibody. IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice induced lethality and, consistently, greatly increased CHIKV viremia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival and viral titer data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: IFNAR1-dependent response did not contribute to the control of CHIKV in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
claims.source: By contrast with results for DENV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), IFNAR1-dependent response did contribute to the control of CHIKV in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between DENV and CHIKV infections in IFNAR1 contribution likely reflects the greater impact of IFN-I signaling in CHIKV versus DENV infection and/or a differential contribution of the alternate IRF-mediated signal transduction.
claims.source: This discrepancy between DENV and CHIKV infections likely reflects the greater impact of IFN-I signaling in CHIKV versus DENV infection and/or a differential contribution of the alternate IRF-mediated signal transduction.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice increased CHIKV titers (~10 fold-increase, although not statistically significant).
claims.source: Similar to DENV, NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice increased CHIKV titers (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, ~10 fold-increase, although not statistically significant).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control two genetically distant RNA viruses (CHIKV and DENV) via the local production of IFN-I and IFNγ secretion by NK cells.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control two genetically distant RNA viruses (CHIKV and DENV) via the local production of IFN-I and IFNγ secretion by NK cells.

results.result: DENV-infected cells activate pDCs through an indirect, contact-dependent mechanism that selectively induces IRF7-mediated IFN-I production without triggering NF-κB-dependent inflammatory cytokine responses (TNFα). This bifurcated response is distinct from direct TLR7 stimulation and is not due to kinetic differences or active inhibition by DENV.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C39 provide converging evidence from human and mouse pDCs showing selective IFN-I/ISG induction without TNFα production in response to DENV-infected cells. The use of IFNβ pretreatment (C33) and control experiments with IMQ (C35) effectively rule out alternative explanations. The data are internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: A novel pDC:Irf7+ mouse model was generated by knocking in Irf7 under the pDC-specific Siglech promoter on an Irf3/7 double knockout background. This model restricts IRF7 expression to pDCs while preserving independent NF-κB signaling and avoiding overexpression artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48 and C121 document the generation and validation of the pDC:Irf7+ model with appropriate molecular, protein, and functional characterization. Flow cytometry (C44), bioassays (C45-C46), and cytokine measurements (C47-C48) confirm pDC-specific IRF7 expression and function. The hemizygous design preserves Siglech expression (C42), and expression levels are controlled (C121).

results.result: In DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, despite undetectable systemic IFN-α/β protein, early ISG induction occurs across multiple tissues at 18h post-infection. This pDC-IRF7 response induces robust ISG expression without NF-κB-dependent inflammatory transcripts, demonstrating complete segregation of these pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C59 demonstrate a paradox resolved by localized IFN-I signaling: undetectable systemic IFN-I (C52) yet robust ISG induction (C53-C54). The data from multiple tissues and time points, combined with segregation of ISG and NF-κB responses (C57-C58), strongly support the conclusion. The lower basal ISG levels in knockout mice (C55) are appropriately explained by prior literature.

results.result: pDC-restricted IRF7 signaling significantly reduces DENV viral titers and RNA levels in spleen and plasma at 42-72h post-infection compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice. This viral control depends on IFN-I/IFNAR1 signaling, as demonstrated by IFNAR blockade experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 and C69-C74 provide viral titer, RNA quantification, and antibody blockade data demonstrating pDC-mediated viral control. The IFNAR blockade experiments (C69-C70, C73) establish mechanistic dependence on type I IFN signaling. The early increase in viral levels (C62) is appropriately discussed as potentially reflecting immune cell recruitment. Statistical significance is demonstrated for key comparisons.

results.result: pDC-IRF7 signaling accelerates the type II IFN response in DENV infection, with Ifng and Gbp2 expression detected as early as 18h and peaking at 28h post-infection in pDC:Irf7+ mice, compared to delayed induction in Irf3/7 DKO mice. This acceleration is temporally associated with viral control.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 and C75 document accelerated type II IFN kinetics with appropriate gene expression markers (Ifng, Gbp2) and protein measurements. The temporal correlation with viral control is demonstrated. The distinction between IFN-I-induced ISGs and IFN-II-specific markers (C65) is appropriately made with literature support. The hypothesis formulation (C68) is reasonable given the data and prior literature.

results.result: NK cells in the spleen are the primary source of IFNγ in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice (~12% of splenic NK cells produce IFNγ). NK cell depletion significantly increases DENV viral titers and reduces IFNγ and type II ISG responses, while not affecting type I ISG levels, establishing NK cells as downstream effectors of pDC-IRF7 signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C86 and C140 provide comprehensive flow cytometry, depletion studies, and molecular analyses demonstrating NK cell-mediated IFNγ production. The depletion efficiency (>80%, C83) is adequate, and the effects on viral titers (C83), IFNγ levels (C84), and ISG responses (C84-C86) are statistically significant. The tissue-specific response (C78-C79) and lack of effect on type I ISGs (C86) support the proposed pathway hierarchy.

results.result: CHIKV activates pDCs through the same mechanism as DENV: contact-dependent, TLR7-mediated sensing of infected cells that induces IRF7-restricted IFN-α production without NF-κB-dependent TNFα responses. This mechanism is independent of the RLR pathway (MAVS).
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 demonstrate that CHIKV shares the same pDC activation mechanism as DENV using multiple experimental approaches: transwell experiments (C89), TLR7-/- pDCs (C90), MAVS-/- pDCs (C91), and cytokine profiling (C92). The data are consistent across human and mouse systems and parallel the DENV findings, supporting the generalizability of the mechanism.

results.result: pDC-restricted IRF7 signaling provides complete protection from lethal CHIKV infection (100% survival in pDC:Irf7+ mice vs. rapid lethality in Irf3/7 DKO mice), with tissue-specific viral control most effective in distal sites (spleen, liver). This protection depends on IFNAR signaling, as demonstrated by antibody blockade inducing lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99, C101-C103, C106, and C130 provide survival data, viral titers across tissues, and IFNAR blockade experiments demonstrating complete protection by pDC-IRF7 signaling. The 100% survival (C95) vs. lethal infection in controls (C94) is striking. The tissue-specific control (C98-C99) and IFNAR dependence (C102) are well-documented. The undetectable IFN-I despite protection (C101) parallels DENV findings and supports localized responses.

results.result: DENV and CHIKV infections show differential outcomes in Irf3/7 DKO mice: CHIKV is invariably lethal while DENV is controlled by 72h post-infection. This difference correlates with viral titer levels and differential sensitivity to type I vs. type II IFN signaling. pDC IFN-I responses provide intermediate viral control for DENV and complete protection for CHIKV.
results.evaluation: Claims C105, C129-C136, and C142 document differential outcomes between DENV and CHIKV with appropriate viral titer measurements and survival data. The correlation with viral load (C133) and differential IFNAR contribution (C134) are demonstrated. The proposed role of alternate IRF proteins (C135-C136) is appropriately speculative. The differential sensitivity to IFN types (C142) is supported by literature citations.

results.result: pDCs are key initiators of antiviral responses to DENV and CHIKV through IRF7-prioritized signaling that excludes NF-κB responses. Despite undetectable systemic IFN-I, pDC-IRF7 signaling induces potent antiviral responses through localized, contact-dependent IFN production that accelerates NK-mediated type II IFN responses and controls viremia while avoiding inflammatory pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111, C120, C123-C124, C126-C127, C150-C151 represent the major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive data from ex vivo experiments, the pDC:Irf7+ model, viral control studies, and mechanistic analyses. The concept of localized IFN responses (C110, C123-C124) explains the paradox of undetectable systemic IFN-I yet robust antiviral effects.

results.result: Background claims establish that type I IFN responses are critical for RNA virus control, pDCs are specialized IFN-I producers, and many viruses including DENV and CHIKV do not directly activate pDCs. Pattern recognition receptors (cytoplasmic and endosomal) recognize viral motifs, and most viruses have evolved evasion mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C12-C15, C18-C19, C23-C24 represent established knowledge in viral immunology supported by general knowledge and appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The claims are accurate representations of the field.

results.result: Prior work has identified alternative pathogen-sensing mechanisms involving pDC sensing of infected cells, including contact-dependent activation by DENV and other viruses. TLR7/9 signaling can show bifurcated patterns with differential IFN-I vs. NF-κB activation depending on subcellular compartmentalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 and C25-C28 accurately cite prior literature establishing the foundation for the current study. The citations to Webster et al., 2016, Décembre et al., 2014, Swiecki and Colonna, 2015, and others are appropriate. These claims provide important context but represent prior work rather than new findings.

results.result: IRF5-dependent ISGs (Mx1, Ifit1) are upregulated in Irf3/7 DKO pDCs, and late ISG induction in Irf3/7 DKO mice is independent of pDC IRF7-mediated IFN-I, likely mediated by IRF1-induced type II IFN. Eventual DENV control in Irf3/7 DKO mice depends on the IFNγ response.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C71-C72, C137-C139 document alternate IRF pathways with appropriate gene expression data and literature support. The late ISG induction (C71) and its independence from pDC-IRF7 signaling are demonstrated. The role of IRF1 (C72) and IFNγ in eventual control (C137-C138) are supported by citations. These findings contextualize the pDC-IRF7 response within broader antiviral immunity.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that neutrophils and monocytes modulate NK cell activation, pDCs are required for control of some but not all viral infections, and pDCs may serve as a failsafe upon systemic infection. NF-κB-dependent cytokines regulate IFNγ production by NK cells, and pDCs act with monocytes to potentiate NK cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C112-C116, C145-C147 accurately cite relevant prior literature with appropriate references (Costa et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2008; Swiecki and Colonna, 2015; Schulthess et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013; García-Sastre, 2017; Tomasello et al., 2014). These provide important context for interpreting the current findings but represent established knowledge.

results.result: The pDC:Irf7+ model offers unique opportunities to define pDC function and study cryptic pDC-mediated control of infections that might be masked by immune homeostasis when pDCs are depleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 represent valid conclusions about the utility of the new mouse model. The model does provide advantages over depletion approaches (C116-C117), and the concept of masked pDC function (C119) is reasonable speculation. These are appropriate interpretive statements about the model's value.

results.result: Siglech expression by pDCs is inversely correlated with ISG upregulation in vivo, and NF-κB induction by DENV/CHIKV in other cell types likely requires cross-talk between IRF3 and NF-κB.
results.evaluation: Claims C122 and C128 provide supporting observations with appropriate data (C122: flow cytometry with citation to Puttur et al., 2013) and reasonable inference (C128: supported by citations to Freaney et al., 2013 and Iwanaszko and Kimmel, 2015). These are valid but secondary findings.

results.result: Speculative interpretations suggest that higher early DENV levels in pDC:Irf7+ mice may reflect immune cell recruitment, pDC responses may control systemic spread, differential IFNAR contributions between DENV and CHIKV may reflect virus-specific sensitivities, and segregating NF-κB and IRF7 responses may have therapeutic potential given the association of NF-κB cytokines with disease severity.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C100, C104, C148-C149 represent speculative interpretations and potential applications. While these are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations (C62: Schmid and Harris, 2014; Seo et al., 2011; C100: Swiecki et al., 2013; C149: Chen et al., 2007; Dupuis-Maguiraga et al., 2012), they are not directly tested in the manuscript and require future validation.

results.result: IFNγ production by NK cells is restricted to the spleen (not blood), suggesting necessity for close apposition to infected/activated cells. pDC-IRF7 signaling is associated with neutrophil recruitment and monocyte activation in the spleen.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C144 document tissue-specific immune responses with appropriate flow cytometry data. The inference about cell-cell proximity requirements (C143) is reasonable given the localized response. The association with neutrophil and monocyte responses (C144) is demonstrated, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: Summary of key findings: DENV and CHIKV infected cells are sensed indirectly by pDCs, resulting in selective IRF7 activation and IFN-I production without inflammatory cytokines. A pDC-restricted IRF7 mouse model was developed, and despite undetectable IFN-I protein, pDC-IRF7 signaling controlled both viruses, protected from lethal CHIKV, and amplified downstream responses including accelerated NK cell-mediated type II IFN.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C11 represent the abstract/summary statements that are supported by the comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript. These high-level conclusions accurately reflect the major findings documented in the detailed results. All key assertions are backed by appropriate experimental evidence.
